description: Six-year-old Scout looks at Maycomb, Alabama. Between childish games and unfair trial, Harper Lee shows how moral courage confronts racism.

hero.hook: A bird that sings without harming: the metaphor of an innocence that society refuses to protect.

blocks.text: Published in **1960**, **Don't Shoot the Mockingbird** is one of the most widely read novels in the United States. **Harper Lee** tells it through the eyes of **Scout**, a six-year-old girl. Scout's real name is Jean Louise Finch. The story takes place in **Maycomb**, a small fictional town in Alabama, during the **Great Depression**. This global economic crisis affected the 1930s.

Between children's games, naive curiosity and legal drama, the book speaks of justice, empathy and courage in the face of racism. Crowned with the **Pulitzer** in **1961**, it remains a central text in English-speaking schools. It is also a mirror of American racial tensions.

**Harper Lee**, born Nelle Harper Lee in **1926** in **Monroeville**, Alabama, modeled Maycomb after her hometown. His father, a local lawyer, had defended two black men accused of murder, as , the central character of the novel, would later do. This biographical experience anchors the story in a reality of the Deep South. [[Atticus Finch]]

blocks.caption: Harper Lee, the author who turned her Alabamian childhood into a global classic.

blocks.text: **Truman Capote**, author of *In Cold Blood*, was Harper Lee's childhood friend in Monroeville. He inspired the character of Dill, the little boy who visits the Finches every summer.

After the dazzling success, Lee chose to withdraw from the media and published almost nothing for decades. In **2015**, shortly before his death,  appeared. This is actually an early draft written before the **1960** version. It presents a more ambiguous Atticus Finch and revives debates on the interpretation of the novel. [[Go and post a sentry]]

blocks.text: The trial of **Tom Robinson**, a black man unjustly accused of assault, occupies the center of the novel. , Scout's father and lawyer, accepts his defense knowing he will lose. In the  South, the skin color of the accused weighs more than physical evidence. [[Atticus Finch]] [[Jim Crow laws and the segregationist South]]

blocks.caption: A Southern courthouse in the 1930s: the place where Scout discovers injustice.

blocks.text: Atticus demonstrates the physical impossibility of the crime, but the jury, composed entirely of white men, convicts Tom. For Scout and her brother Jem, it's a shock: the law exists, but justice can fail. Atticus teaches empathy: “you only really know someone by putting yourself in their shoes.” True courage, he says, is to fight even when you know you have lost in advance.

sections.title: Atticus Finch and the Sacrifice of Justice

blocks.text: Atticus forbids killing the **mockingbird**. In English, we say *mockingbird*. He does no harm, he sings for others. The metaphor targets **Tom Robinson** and **Boo Radley**, two harmless beings that society persecutes or transforms into monsters. To kill a mockingbird is to destroy an innocence that only asks to live.
In several French editions, the title was *When the nightingale*, because the mockingbird does not exist in Europe, although it is not the same species.

**Boo Radley**, a hermit feared by the neighbors, is presented as a ghost by the children. However, he secretly protects Scout and Jem. When he saves the children from an attacker at the end, Scout understands that he is not a monster, but a shy man who has been distorted by rumor. Heroism can be silent, invisible, like that of Atticus in the face of a system that he cannot overthrow alone.

sections.title: The mockingbird: symbolism of broken innocence

Critics also see the character of Atticus as a . This is a narrative trope where a white character “saves” black characters. The story is seen from the white side and leaves little voice to the black characters, who remain in the background. These debates enrich reading without erasing the impact of the book on generations of readers. [[white savior]]
